Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Nothing says true love like releasing a caged butterfly, don't you think? Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin are to be paid $5 million for the picture rights to their wedding. The butterflies are reported to be the piece-de-resistance of England's most anticipated celebrity wedding of the year. Wayne Rooney, the best English footballer of his generation, and Coleen McLoughlin, his High School sweetheart, were to marry in an estimated $10 million ceremony in Italy Thursday. As they kiss, guests are apparently meant to open boxes and release the butterflies. The moment has been pilloried widely in the British media, tacky and over the top they all think, but is it just sour grapes? It has been a long and, at times, bumpy road for the couple to the altar. One littered with fierce criticism from the British press, which has enjoyed nothing more than lampooning Rooney and McLoughlin for being 'common.' The Daily Mail once even asked: "Is this Britain's ghastliest couple?" Rooney has been dubbed "Shrek" and "Mr Potato Head" due to his looks and his background as the son of a school dinner lady who grew up on a council estate is often referred to in a disparaging way. McLoughlin, meanwhile, has been subjected to page upon page of bitter stories about her weight, shopping sprees and her lack of closeness to Victoria Beckham. There has also been fierce criticism over the fact she has managed to become a millionaire in her own right. It's all down to Rooney apparently, and nothing to do with her appearing to be quite a decent person, who did well at school and has cleverly managed to parlay some of her fame into various media and advertising projects. Anyone who has seen her television show -- Coleen's Real Women -- can see she is a decent, bubbly person, who is very good at putting people at ease. Much to the media's fury, the couple have sold the rights to cover the wedding to OK magazine for a record $5 million. However they're not pocketing all the cash themselves, with an undisclosed sum from the fee to be donated to the Claire House children's hospice in Cheshire -- where McLoughlin's disabled foster sister Rosie is cared for. The queen's grandson, Peter Phillips and his bride Autumn Kelly, recently received $1m from Hello magazine to cover their wedding but they didn't receive an eighth of the opprobrium now directed at the more generous, but lower class, Rooney and McLoughlin. Moreover, in lieu of presents, Rooney and McLoughlin have also asked guests to donate money to the Alder Hey children's hospital in Liverpool. The wedding might be over the top, with a private yacht and luxury jet for guests (they are covering the guests' costs), expensive plonk and a $200,000 wedding dress, but at least the couple have worked hard for what they have. Their success despite a working-class background appears to be the greatest source of frustration for critics. It's just not on that someone who wasn't born into privilege and didn't go to a posh school can enjoy their wealth. That would be ugly. If anything, the couple's relationship and success is a triumph over adversity. They have known each other since McLoughlin was 12, but she spent two years fending off Rooney's entreaties to go out on a date. He finally got his chance when he saw her struggling to fix a broken bicycle chain. He rode over to help, popped the question again and got a yes. Surely they should be congratulated for creating their own modern fairytale complete with butterflies? The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

McLoughlin, meanwhile, has endured page after page of unkind commentary regarding her weight, her shopping habits, and her supposed lack of closeness with Victoria Beckham. When English footballer Wayne Rooney married his longtime sweetheart Coleen McLoughlin, the event was destined to become one of the most talked-about celebrity weddings in recent British memory. The couple, who had been together since their teenage years, spared no expense in creating a spectacle that captured the imagination—and the scorn—of the nation's press.

For two people who had risen to fame and fortune from ordinary backgrounds, the wedding represented both a personal milestone and a very public statement of their arrival among Britain's elite.

Yet the celebration did not escape the sharp tongues of the British media. Much of the coverage carried an unmistakably classist undertone, with commentators mocking the couple as "common" and dismissing the elaborate festivities as "ghastly." This criticism reflected a broader tendency within certain sections of the press to look down on newly wealthy figures from working-class origins, judging their tastes and lifestyle choices against snobbish standards of what constitutes "proper" refinement.

Despite this barrage of mockery, the Rooneys had the last laugh in financial terms. The couple secured a record-breaking deal reportedly worth $5 million for the exclusive rights to their wedding photographs—a sum that underscored just how commercially valuable their images remained. This staggering figure exposed a striking contradiction at the heart of the media's treatment of the pair: even as journalists ridiculed them as vulgar and unsophisticated, the public's appetite for glimpses into their lives remained insatiable.

Ultimately, the Rooney wedding illustrated the peculiar tension that defines modern celebrity culture. On one hand, the couple faced relentless snobbery and derision; on the other, their genuine popularity and undeniable financial success proved that the very media outlets that mocked them were also profiting from, and helping to sustain, their fame. In the end, the mockery did little to diminish their standing—if anything, it only confirmed how firmly the Rooneys had established themselves as figures of enduring public fascination.

counterfactuals.output:
# In Defense of the Rooneys: Why We Should Celebrate, Not Condemn, a Working-Class Love Story

*An opinion piece*

There is something deeply revealing about the British media's treatment of Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin's wedding—and what it reveals is not about the couple, but about us.

When the young footballer and his childhood sweetheart married in a lavish Italian ceremony, the reaction from certain quarters of the press was as predictable as it was unbecoming. The words came fast and sneering: "vulgar," "excessive," "chavish." The releasing of butterflies during the celebration was mocked. The reported £2.5 million OK! magazine deal was treated as evidence of crass commercialism. And through it all ran an ugly undercurrent that had less to do with the wedding itself than with where its stars came from.

Let us be honest about what's really happening here.

## The Butterflies and the Snobbery

Take the derided butterflies. A romantic flourish at a wedding—hardly a novel concept—became fodder for columnists eager to prove their sophistication by mocking someone else's. One suspects that had an aristocratic couple or an established celebrity dynasty released butterflies, the same writers would have called it "whimsical" or "enchanting."

The difference, of course, is that Rooney is the son of a laborer from Croxteth, and Coleen grew up in the same working-class Liverpool neighborhood. Their crime, in the eyes of their critics, is not that they spent money, but that they are the *wrong sort* of people to have it.

## The OK! Deal: Pragmatism, Not Greed

The magazine deal deserves particular scrutiny—not because it warrants criticism, but because the criticism itself is so hypocritical. Selling exclusive rights to a wedding is standard practice among the famous, from Hollywood stars to European royalty. It offers a practical solution to an impossible problem: how do you celebrate a private moment when paparazzi will pursue you regardless?

By choosing a controlled arrangement, the couple protected their guests, retained some dignity over how their day was presented, and—crucially—directed the proceeds where their harshest critics rarely look.

## The Part the Critics Conveniently Ignore

Because here is what gets lost beneath the sneering headlines: their charitable giving.

The Rooneys have quietly supported causes that matter to them, including donations connected to Alder Hey Children's Hospital and other charitable efforts. A young couple, barely out of their teens, chose to think beyond themselves at the very moment the world told them to think only of their own celebration.

Where were the celebratory headlines for that? Why does generosity earn a fraction of the coverage that a butterfly earns in mockery?

## What This Says About Us

The truth is that Wayne Rooney and Coleen McLoughlin represent something the British establishment has never been entirely comfortable with: working-class success on working-class terms. They did not apologize for their roots or sand down their edges to please tastemakers. They celebrated their love the way they wanted to, spent money they had earned, and gave generously in the process.

We should be capable of a simple, decent response: congratulations. Instead, too many chose contempt—and in doing so, revealed far more about their own prejudices than about any newlywed couple's taste in wedding décor.

The Rooneys owe their critics nothing. Perhaps it is the critics who owe them an apology.

---

*The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a commentary about a celebrity footballer's wedding that challenges the class snobbery in the British press coverage of the couple.
counterfactuals.output:
# When Love Trumps Lineage: The Press, the Pitch, and Their Persistent Snobbery

There is a peculiar ritual that unfolds whenever a footballer marries. The cameras arrive, the columns fill, and beneath the veneer of celebration runs a current of something less generous—a barely concealed sneer at people who have committed the apparent crime of being working-class and successful.

This week's wedding coverage has followed the familiar script. The venue was "ostentatious." The dress was "over-the-top." The guest list was "flashy." Read between the lines and the message is unmistakable: *these people don't know how to behave. They have money but not manners, wealth but not worth.*

## The Vocabulary of Disdain

Notice the words. When old money spends lavishly, it is "traditional" and "tasteful." When a footballer from a council estate does the same, it becomes "gaudy" and "nouveau." The aristocrat's country pile is "characterful"; the footballer's mansion is "garish." The same champagne, the same flowers, the same expense—judged by entirely different standards depending on the accent and the postcode of the people enjoying them.

This is not criticism. It is class policing dressed up as taste.

## What Exactly Is the Offence?

Strip away the coded language and ask what these couples have actually done wrong. A young man of extraordinary talent has worked, from childhood, to reach the pinnacle of the most competitive profession on earth. His bride has built a career, a business, a public life of her own. They have fallen in love. They have chosen to celebrate that love generously, surrounded by their families.

The unforgivable sin, it seems, is not knowing their place—or rather, refusing to stay in it.

The British class system has always reserved a special resentment for those who climb. We claim to love an underdog, but we prefer them grateful and deferential, cap in hand. The moment they buy the big house and wear the expensive watch, our affection curdles into contempt.

## The Bride Bears the Brunt

It is worth noting who absorbs the cruellest coverage. The footballer earns grudging respect for his talent; his wife receives the full force of the snobbery. She is dismissed as a "WAG"—a term designed to reduce an accomplished woman to an accessory. Her ambition is "social climbing." Her intelligence goes unremarked. Her every choice is scrutinised for evidence that she doesn't belong.

We would never speak this way about a duchess. The difference is not conduct. The difference is class.

## A Mirror Worth Holding

Perhaps the discomfort these weddings provoke says less about the couple than about us. They represent something the establishment finds genuinely threatening: proof that talent and determination can breach walls once thought impassable, that the sons and daughters of the working class can build lives of comfort and joy without asking anyone's permission.

That, surely, is worth celebrating rather than sneering at.

So let the press run its snide captions and its knowing asides. The rest of us might simply choose to see what is actually there: two people, in love, marking the occasion as they see fit. Their money is their own. Their happiness is theirs. And their right to enjoy both, without apology, is not diminished by where they started.

The only thing genuinely in poor taste this week is the coverage.

counterfactuals.output:
# The Real Snobbery Behind the Sneering at Wayne and Coleen

There is a particular kind of contempt reserved in Britain for people who came from nothing and had the audacity to enjoy their success. Nowhere has this been clearer than in the way certain quarters of the press and public have treated Wayne and Coleen Rooney—two people from working-class Liverpool who became wealthy and, crucially, refused to apologise for it.

## What the Mockery Really Says

The criticism is rarely stated plainly, because to state it plainly would expose it. Instead it arrives coded in the language of "taste." The wedding was too lavish. The reported magazine deal was too vulgar. The clothes, the cars, the holidays—all of it deemed somehow *too much*. The word that hovers unspoken behind every raised eyebrow is "common."

But notice what is actually being objected to. Wealthy people spend extravagantly on weddings constantly. Aristocrats have staged displays of opulence for centuries and been praised for their "heritage" and "grandeur." When old money spends, it is called elegance. When a footballer's family from a council estate spends, it is called garish. The money is the same. The judgement is entirely about where the person came from.

## Old Money's Unwritten Rules

British class prejudice has always operated on a cruel double standard. It is acceptable to be rich—provided you inherited it, or at least learned to hide it behind the right accent, the right schools, and a studied pretence that you don't really care about it at all. Understatement is the aristocratic virtue precisely because it signals that wealth is nothing new to you.

People who earn their money in a single generation cannot play this game, and are punished for it. Their enjoyment of success is treated as proof they don't deserve it. The very visibility of their achievement—the thing that should be celebrated as social mobility—becomes the charge against them.

## Success Without Permission

What truly rankles about the Rooneys, I suspect, is that they succeeded without asking anyone's permission and without changing who they were. They did not soften their accents, disown their roots, or pretend to have refined tastes acquired at some finishing school. They remained recognisably, unapologetically working class while becoming enormously successful.

For a certain kind of snob, this is intolerable. Social mobility is acceptable in the abstract, as a policy goal to nod along to. It becomes uncomfortable when actual working-class people arrive in spaces of wealth and refuse to perform the gratitude and self-erasure expected of them.

## The Convenient Cover of "Celebrity Culture"

Some will object that this is not about class at all, but about the excesses of celebrity or a legitimate distaste for tabloid spectacle. There is a genuine conversation to be had about celebrity culture. But it is telling how selectively that critique is applied, and how quickly it curdles into personal contempt aimed at a young woman's clothes or a young man's background rather than at the media machine profiting from them both.

We should be honest about what we are watching. A couple from working-class Liverpool built extraordinary success and chose to enjoy it on their own terms. The sneering that followed tells us far more about the enduring snobbery of British society than it ever did about them.

If we genuinely believe in social mobility, we cannot only celebrate it when the newly successful behave as though they are embarrassed to have arrived. Real equality means letting people from working-class backgrounds succeed—and letting them enjoy it—without demanding they apologise for where they came from.

---

*This op-ed presents one argumentative perspective. A fuller treatment might also weigh counterarguments about privacy, media dynamics, and public interest.*

# When Love Meets Limelight: In Defense of the Wedding Everyone Loves to Judge

*Why the year's most talked-about "I do" deserves a little less side-eye and a lot more champagne*

---

There are two kinds of people in this world: those who claim they don't care about celebrity weddings, and those who are lying. This year's main event—a union so lavish it reportedly required its own zip code—has given us all a masterclass in the fine art of pretending we're above it while frantically refreshing the tabloids.

Let's get the eye-watering details out of the way, shall we?

## The Numbers That Broke the Internet (and a Few Budgets)

Sources close to the couple—and by "close," I mean the florist's cousin's Instagram—suggest the celebration spanned three days, two continents, and one very confused flock of doves trained to release rose petals on command. The floral budget alone allegedly rivaled the GDP of a small principality. There were, by most accounts, seventeen thousand peonies, hand-selected because roses were deemed "too on the nose."

The dress? A closely guarded secret requiring the couturier to sign a nondisclosure agreement so airtight it could have withstood a submarine descent. The cake stood taller than several of the guests and, per legend, contained edible gold flakes that cost more per ounce than the actual metal.

And the guest list read like the seating chart at heaven's most exclusive dinner party.

## Now, About All That Judgment

Here's where I lose the cynics.

Somewhere around the third viral post decrying the "obscene excess" of it all, I found myself wondering: since when did we decide that success comes with a mandatory vow of visible modesty?

We celebrate these people when they win. We stream their work, buy their tickets, plaster their faces across our screens and lunchboxes. We built the pedestal, hauled them up onto it, and then act scandalized when they have the audacity to throw a nice party from the top.

The truth is, both halves of this couple clawed their way up through years of rejection, ramen dinners, and the particular indignity of being told they'd "never make it." They earned every peony. If two people who fell in love in the pressure cooker of public life want to celebrate that improbable, fragile, beautiful thing with all the extravagance they can muster—who exactly are we to hand them a spreadsheet and suggest they'd have been happier at the courthouse?

## The Quiet Case for Joy

There's something almost radical about the whole affair, if you squint. In a moment when we're all encouraged to shrink, to apologize, to caption our happiness with self-deprecation lest anyone accuse us of *enjoying ourselves too loudly*—here are two people saying, without irony: *We are in love, we worked hard, and we are going to celebrate accordingly.*

Is it a lot? Absolutely. Weddings are supposed to be a lot. That's the entire point. A wedding is a defiant declaration that despite the divorce statistics, the cynicism, and the odds—two people are betting on forever anyway. When you frame it that way, seventeen thousand peonies start to look less like waste and more like a very expensive act of hope.

## Let Them Eat (Gold-Flecked) Cake

So when the think pieces roll in—and roll in they will—declaring the whole spectacle a symbol of everything wrong with modern excess, I'll be over here, glass raised, thinking a simpler thought.

Good for them.

May the marriage outlast the news cycle. May the peonies have been worth it. And may the rest of us find something in our own lives worth celebrating with even a fraction of that shameless, gorgeous, unapologetic joy.

Now if you'll excuse me, I have a tabloid to refresh. Purely for research.

# When Love Takes Flight: What the Media Got Wrong About the Rooney-McLoughlin Wedding

*A CNN Commentary*

The butterflies rose first.

Before the vows, before the first dance, before any of the moments that would later fill the tabloids, a cloud of monarchs lifted into the afternoon air—a shimmer of orange and black against a bright sky. Guests tilted their faces upward. For a few seconds, everyone simply watched something beautiful ascend.

Then the mockery began.

## The Easy Cynicism of the Modern Media

Within hours, the butterfly release had become a punchline. Commentators called it "over-the-top." Social media accounts screenshotted the moment for ridicule. The coverage that followed reduced a wedding into a caricature—too lavish here, too sentimental there, too *much* of whatever the internet had decided to be unimpressed by that week.

This is a familiar reflex. Cynicism costs nothing and generates clicks. It is far easier to sneer at a symbol than to ask what it might mean to the people who chose it. And in the rush to score points, the coverage skipped past the actual human beings at the center of the day.

That is worth pausing on—because the Rooney-McLoughlin story deserves better than a punchline.

## A Love Story That Predates the Cameras

Long before anyone was live-tweeting their reception, the couple's relationship was the ordinary, patient kind that rarely makes headlines. They met young. They stayed together through the awkward years and the uncertain ones, through the seasons when neither had anything to prove and no one was watching.

By the time the world took notice, they had already built the foundation that the wedding was meant to celebrate. The theatricality that critics mocked wasn't a performance for an audience. It was the exuberance of two people who had waited a long time to stand in front of everyone they loved and say so out loud.

There is a difference between spectacle and celebration. The media, in its haste, seems to have forgotten how to tell them apart.

## The Part the Coverage Skipped

Here is what most of the commentary left out: the wedding was not only about the couple.

Rather than a traditional gift registry, they asked guests to contribute to causes they had spent years quietly supporting. Their charitable work—the kind that doesn't come with photographers—has run through their relationship as steadily as the relationship itself. The same generosity that critics mocked as excess was, in fact, pointed outward, toward people who would never attend a wedding like this one.

Those butterflies, it turns out, weren't just a flourish. For the couple, the release carried meaning tied to renewal and remembrance—a gesture rooted in something personal, not staged for approval.

## What We Reveal When We Mock

It is telling that a monarch butterfly, one of nature's genuine marvels, could be transformed into an object of derision simply because two people dared to find it meaningful.

The instinct to mock says less about the Rooney-McLoughlin wedding than it does about us. We have grown fluent in irony and clumsy with sincerity. We treat earnestness as an invitation to ridicule, as though caring openly about anything were the real embarrassment.

But love, when it is genuine, is not embarrassing. Neither is joy. Neither is a couple choosing to mark their happiness by giving something away.

The butterflies are long gone now, scattered to wherever butterflies go. What remains is a simpler truth the coverage missed entirely: two people who loved each other, who wanted others to share in that love, and who used their happiest day to lift someone else.

That deserves applause—not a punchline.
